newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall; dollar surges.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall; dollar surges.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks edged lower on Friday as the market took a breather after this week's series of record closing highs driven by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments about the economy.
Bonds also fell, but the dollar surged to its highest level against the Swiss franc in four years and rose against the German mark for a fifth day in a row.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 3.49 points lower at 8,113.44, pausing after three straight record closes. For the week, the index was up 222.98 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,393 to 1,378 on moderate volume of 519 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said the market appeared a bit fatigued but showed little indication that its broad, powerhouse rally was approaching a significant top.

"Quite frankly, I think we're due for a rest here," said James Crawford, senior vice president at Trevor Stewart Burton & Jacobsen Inc. "But I certainly don't think this a period when one has to run for cover."

There were pockets of nervous activity in the market, particularly among shares in personal computer makers. That group, which has rallied fiercely of late, saw its fortunes reverse after one of the companies, Gateway 2000 Inc., posted uninspiring earnings.
Analysts said they were not surprised at the severity of the group's fall, given investors' mercurial attitude to high technology stocks.
"We've seen them go through some pretty dramatic swings," said Ken Tower, technical analyst at UST Securities. "I don't think anyone is going to want to hold them for the ride down."
But the selling was narrowly focused and the technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index managed to scratch out a marginal gain, closing up 0.45 of a point to 1,569.58.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury fell 7/32, or $2.1875 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.46 percent from 6.44 percent at Thursday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar set another six-year high against the mark, rising to an intraday peak of 1.8403 and ending at 1.8378 marks, up from 1.8348 Thursday.

It rose to 0.8262 Swiss francs -- its highest level since August 1993 -- before settling at 1.5160 against 1.5065. Against the yen, the dollar rose as high as 116.99 and ended at 116.95 vs. 116.05 Thursday.
Gasoline prices rose sharply amid strong demand, tightening supplies and the rising price of a key gasoline blending component.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline for August delivery settled 1.82 cents higher at 64.03 cents a gallon.
Gasoline's rally swept the rest of the oil complex higher, with September crude settling 12 cents higher at $19.89 a barrel and August heating oil finishing 0.60 cent a gallon up at 53.99 cents.

Copper prices rose on heavy fund shortcovering, aided by strength in the other base metals, particularly zinc and nickel. At New York's Commodity Exchange, copper for September delivery closed at 111.45 cents a pound, up 3.65 cents.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange lumber prices were stronger, supported by news that British Columbia's coastal forest companies had cancelled contract talks with the lumber workers' union, dealers said.
Lumber for September delivery closed up $1.10 at $346.60 per thousand board feet.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,851.5, down 11.4 points, or 0.23 percent. The index was down 25.7 from last week. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,389.54, up 103.31 points, or 0.51 percent. This was up 140.22 from last Friday.
